body.text: On November 19, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman indirectly blamed India for the ongoing violent unrest in Bangladesh.

Speaking at a public event in Lalmonirhat district in northern Bangladesh, bordering India, Rahman accused the banned Awami League of resorting to violence and arson. He then went on to say that “the country across the border, where they have fled to, is their master … To satisfy those masters, they have again started conspiring against Bangladesh, and its people,” Reuters reported.

Although the Bangladeshi prime minister did not name “the country across the border,” the jibe was undoubtedly aimed at India, which surrounds Bangladesh on three sides and has had a warm relationship with the Awami League for decades. In his speech in parliament the previous day, Rahman had criticized India for “sheltering and supporting fugitive Awami League leaders and using them to destabilise Bangladesh,” Dhaka Tribune reported.

Since the fall of the Awami League government on August 5, 2024, several Awami League leaders, including former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, have been living in India. In November last year, Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity committed by her government during the violent crackdown on students participating in the 2024 mass protests.

In August this year, Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh by December. Earlier this month, she applied for a new passport and a national identity card to facilitate her travel back home. But the Rahman government rejected her request, saying “Bangladesh does not issue passports to terrorists.”

The Awami League responded to Dhaka’s refusal to give Hasina a passport by calling for nationwide protests that unfolded last week in violent clashes, bomb blasts and arson. It was against this backdrop that Rahman pointed an accusing finger at India.

India has avoided reacting to Rahman’s jibe. The Ministry of External Affairs said it had “no comments to offer on the internal developments in Bangladesh.” India is keen to have a “positive, constructive, and forward-looking relationship” with Bangladesh, it said
India-Bangladesh relations were warm when the Awami League was in power. However, with Hasina ousted, ties frayed during the interim administration under Muhammad Yunus.

Although previous Bangladesh Nationalist Party governments were hostile to India – they had allowed anti-India militants to operate out of Bangladesh – Rahman’s swearing-in as prime minister in February evoked “cautious optimism” in India. Rahman seemed keen “to chart a new path” in Bangladesh’s relations with India, Smruti Pattanaik, a research fellow at the New Delhi-based Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analysis, told The Diplomat.
However, in the nine months since Rahman took charge, Dhaka-Delhi relations remain frayed.

Rahman has made state visits to Malaysia, China and Japan, met with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in New York to discuss trade and defense cooperation, and struck defense deals with Türkiye.
However, he is yet to visit India.
This is because Dhaka has made the improvement of India-Bangladesh relations and a visit by Rahman to India contingent on Delhi extraditing Hasina to Bangladesh.

“The Rahman government has made Hasina the core factor determining its relations with New Delhi,” Pattanaik said, adding that it has “made Hasina a bilateral issue between India and Bangladesh, when she is, in fact, Bangladesh’s problem.”
Rahman is reportedly under pressure from anti-India and anti-Awami League hardliners in his government and the opposition parties to not visit India.

Both the interim administration and the BNP government have repeatedly called on India to extradite Hasina to Bangladesh, but India has not responded. “The BNP government would like India to rein in Hasina, which India will not,” Pattanaik said.

In August, for example, Dhaka warned India against allowing Hasina to address a press conference in Delhi, saying that it would “harm” bilateral relations. The press event happened, albeit with Hasina delivering her speech virtually. Bangladesh expressed “outrage.”

Hasina puts India in a dilemma. Keeping her in India provides “permanent fuel for anti-India sentiment” among Bangladeshis. If she is sent back, India’s relations with Bangladesh could improve. But sending Hasina, a long-time ally of India, back to Bangladesh, where she would be jailed and possibly hanged, will send a message to India’s friends that it is not a reliable ally.

Hasina puts the Rahman government in a bind, too. If it doesn’t push for Hasina’s return to Bangladesh, opposition parties, especially the Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party will take the matter to the streets, piling on pressure on the already beleaguered government.

However, Hasina’s return to Bangladesh could adversely impact the BNP’s political fortunes. Hasina continues to have support in Bangladesh, and her return will galvanize her party and uplift the sagging spirits of her supporters. It will give the Awami League a fresh lease of life, with implications for the BNP’s electoral fortunes. Officially, the Rahman government has said Hasina should return to face punishment. The Jamaat-e-Islami can be expected to mobilize street demonstrations to push the government to hang Hasina. But can Rahman have her executed? Will the government take the risk of hanging the daughter of Bangladesh’s founding father, Sheikh Mujibur Rehman?
Consequently, for all the noise it is making about Hasina’s return to Bangladesh, the Rahman government may not be keen on her coming back.
“If it were, all it needs to do is issue her a passport and she will return home,” Indian officials told The Diplomat, pointing out that Hasina is a “willing returnee.”
Rahman understands well that Delhi will not extradite Hasina to Bangladesh and is therefore insisting that Delhi extradite her to Bangladesh.

The Rahman government is under tremendous pressure at home. The law and order situation has deteriorated. Islamists are on the rise. Bangladesh’s ready-made garments sector, which is its main forex earner, is on strike. The economy is in trouble. Improving ties with India could help Dhaka address some of these problems, especially the energy crisis. But Rahman’s hands are tied, it seems.

In their bid to absolve themselves of responsibility, many leaders have blamed a “foreign hand” for their domestic problems. It’s an old refuge that leaders take to deflect attention from their own shortcomings.
By pointing to “the country across the border,” Rahman is simply taking a leaf from their book.
